paper.title: Complete Policy Regret Bounds for Tallying Bandits

unmapped: m-memory bounded adaptive adversary: mean loss of action x is an unknown arbitrary function h_x(y) of the tally y of plays of x in the last m rounds (rested-bandit / deterministic MDP structure)
regret is complete policy regret against the best length-T action sequence
settings.definition_quote: An online learning game is an $(m,g,h)$-tallying bandit if the adversary is $m$-memory bounded, $g$-restricted and $h$-tallying, and if after playing action $a_t$ the player observes a random variable $\widetilde{h}_{a_t}(y_t) \in [0,1]$ satisfying $\E [ \widetilde{h}_{a_t}(y_t) ] = h_{a_t}(y_t) = g_{a_t}(a_{\max \{ 1, t-m+1 \}:t}) = f_t(a_{1:t})$

unmapped: m-memory bounded tallying adversary: mean loss h_x(y) depends on tally of x in last m rounds
complete policy regret against best length-T action sequence
settings.definition_quote: When the player plays action $x$, and this action $x$ has been played a total of $y$ times in the past $m$ timesteps (including the current timestep), then the player receives as feedback a Bernoulli random variable with mean $h_x(y)$.

unmapped: m-memory bounded tallying adversary with losses h_x(y) in [0,1]
complete policy regret against best length-T action sequence
settings.definition_quote: let us consider the simplified setting of deterministic bandit feedback, where for each $t, a_{1:t} \in \ActSet^t$ the player observes $f_t(a_{1:t})$ with no noise.

settings.name_in_paper: online learning against oblivious adversary, complete policy regret (full information)
unmapped: comparator is the best per-round action sequence (complete policy class)
settings.definition_quote: Let $\ActSet = \{ x_1, x_2 \}$. To define its sequence of loss functions, the adversary first samples a bit string $b$ uniformly at random from $\{ 0, 1 \}^T$.

settings.name_in_paper: m-memory bounded g-restricted adversary, complete policy regret (full information)
unmapped: adversary is m-memory bounded and g-restricted (time-invariant loss as function of last m actions)
complete policy regret against best length-T action sequence
settings.definition_quote: An $m$-memory bounded adversary is said to be $g$-restricted if the following is true. For each action $x \in \ActSet$, there exists a base function $g_x: \cup_{m'=1}^m \ActSet^{m'} \to [0,1]$, such that $f_t(a_{1:t}) = g_{a_t}(a_{\max \{ 1, t-m+1 \}:t})$.

source.quote:
For any $(m,g,h)$-tallying bandit problem and any input $\delta \in (0,1)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ the complete policy regret of Algorithm~ef{alg:main} (SE-TB) is upper bounded as $\cpReg \leq 1200 
umact m \sqrt{T} ( \sqrt{ \log ( 2 
umact m \log(T) / \delta ) } + \log_2 ( \sqrt{T} / (2 
umact m) ) )$.

results.notes: Complete policy regret vs best length-T action sequence, defined via mean losses f_t. Algorithm is computationally inefficient (enumerates K^sqrt(T) cyclic policies), hence compute=exponential.

conditions: m at least some sufficiently large universal constant (proof)
K larger than some numerical constant (via Proposition 1)

source.label: thm:lower
source.quote: There exists an $(m,g,h)$-tallying bandit problem and a numerical constant $c > 0$, such that the (expected) complete policy regret of any (possibly randomized) algorithm on this problem is lower bounded as $\E [ \cpReg ] \geq c \cdot \max \{ m \numact, \sqrt{m \numact T} \}$.

results.notes: Expected complete policy regret where the comparator's loss uses mean losses; recorded as pseudo_regret. Hard instance uses Bernoulli feedback.

source.label: prop1
source.quote: Consider any $(m,g,h)$-tallying bandit problem with deterministic bandit feedback. Then the complete policy regret of Algorithm~\ref{alg:alg_det} ($\mathbb{ALG}_{\text{det}}$) is almost surely upper bounded as $\cpReg \leq (m+1) \numact$.

results.notes: Offline planning step may be computationally expensive; paper says statistically feasible.

conditions: K larger than some numerical constant (proof)

source.label: prop1
source.quote: Moreover, there exists an $(m,g,h)$-tallying bandit problem, such that the (expected) complete policy regret of any (possibly randomized) algorithm on this problem with deterministic feedback is lower bounded as $\E [ \cpReg ] \geq m \numact / 128$.

results.notes: Deterministic feedback, so regret types coincide; expectation over algorithm randomness and random instance.

source.label: counterexample1
source.quote: Attaining sublinear complete policy regret is then equivalent to making a sublinear number of mistakes when guessing the value of $b_t$. Since this is impossible, we have that $\E [ \cpReg ] = \bigomega(T)$

results.notes: Informal counterexample; with oblivious adversary the complete policy class comparator is the best action each round. Paper writes Omega-tilde; holds under full information.

source.label: counterexample2
source.quote: Meanwhile, suffering zero loss for the player is at least as hard as identifying $b$, and a standard ``needle in the haystack'' argument shows that this requires $\bigomega(2^m)$ timesteps. Hence we have that $\E [ \cpReg ] = \bigomega(\min \{ 2^m, T \} / m)$

results.notes: Informal counterexample argument; holds even with full information.
